title: US Bifurcation, aging, and job growth are shaping the metro consumer outlook
author: Emma Pollard
text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

17 Nov 2026

US Bifurcation, aging, and job growth are shaping the metro consumer outlook

Household spending power has become more concentrated over time

Although AI-related investment has been a major driver of US growth over the past year, consumer spending remains the backbone of the economy. Identifying which households, spending categories, and locations are powering spending is crucial to pinpointing opportunities for B2C companies.

Spending has become more reliant on high-income, asset-rich households, buoyed by equity and housing wealth, while lower-income households have struggled. This bifurcation has likely been heightened by the inflation shock from the US-Israel war with Iran and will continue to influence spending going forward.

Another trend that will shape spending is the aging of the population. As seniors gradually take up a greater share of the population, where they live and what they buy will matter more for spending growth.

Although high-income metros (e.g., San Jose) and retiree hotspots (e.g., The Villages) feature toward the top of our medium-term spending growth rankings, many of the top performers are still those with the strongest job growth prospects (e.g., Austin), most of which are located in the Sun Belt. By contrast, several Northeast and Midwest metros are forecast to lag, hindered by sluggish employment and population prospects, and in some cases, exposure to the spike in the price of essentials.

Slower-growing but large metros should not be dismissed as offering limited opportunities. The sheer size of cities like Chicago means that lower growth rates can still translate into huge spending level gains.

We expect discretionary categories (e.g., recreation and culture) and health to record the fastest growth over the medium term, supported by high-income households and seniors, respectively.
